{{Short description|Nonlinear optical process}}
{{Distinguish|two-photon absorption}}
{{redirect|Frequency doubling|the radio technology process|Frequency multiplier}}
[[File:Energy level scheme of SHG.png|200px|thumb|right|Energy level scheme of SHG process]]

'''Second-harmonic generation''' ('''SHG'''), also known as '''frequency doubling''', is the lowest-order wave-wave nonlinear interaction that occurs in various systems, including optical, radio, atmospheric, and magnetohydrodynamic systems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=He |first1=Maosheng |last2=Forbes |first2=Jeffrey M. |date=2022-12-07 |title=Rossby wave second harmonic generation observed in the middle atmosphere |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=7544 |doi=10.1038/s41467-022-35142-3  |doi-access=free|issn=2041-1723 |pmc=9729661 |pmid=36476614|bibcode=2022NatCo..13.7544H }}</ref> As a prototype behavior of waves, SHG is widely used, for example, in doubling laser frequencies. SHG was initially discovered as a [[nonlinear optics|nonlinear optical]] process<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Franken |first1=P. A. |last2=Hill |first2=A. E. |last3=Peters |first3=C. W. |last4=Weinreich |first4=G. |date=1961-08-15 |title=Generation of Optical Harmonics |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=118–119 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118|bibcode=1961PhRvL...7..118F |doi-access=free }}</ref> in which two [[photon]]s with the same frequency interact with a nonlinear material, are "combined", and generate a new photon with twice the energy of the initial photons (equivalently, twice the [[frequency]] and half the [[wavelength]]), that conserves the [[Coherence (physics)|coherence]] of the excitation. It is a special case of two-photon [[sum-frequency generation]], and more generally of [[harmonic generation]].

The second-order [[nonlinear susceptibility]] of a medium characterizes its tendency to cause SHG. Second-harmonic generation, like other even-order nonlinear optical phenomena, is not allowed in media with inversion symmetry (within the leading electric dipole contribution).<ref name=Boyd2007>{{cite book |language=en |title=Nonlinear optics |url=https://archive.org/details/nonlinearopticst00boyd |url-access=limited |chapter=The Nonlinear Optical Susceptibility |year=2007 |last1=Boyd |first1=R. |pages=1–67 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-369470-6.00001-0 |isbn=978-0-12-369470-6 |s2cid=15660817 |edition=third }}</ref> However, effects such as the [[Bloch–Siegert shift]], which occurs when two-level systems are driven at Rabi frequencies comparable to their transition frequencies, can give rise to second-harmonic generation in centrosymmetric systems.<ref>

In some cases, almost 100% of the light energy can be converted to the second-harmonic frequency. These cases typically involve intense pulsed laser beams passing through large crystals and careful alignment to obtain [[phase matching]]. In other cases, like [[second-harmonic imaging microscopy]], only a tiny fraction of the light energy is converted to the second harmonic, but this light can nevertheless be detected with the help of [[optical filter]]s.

[[File:Schematic of the SHG conversion of an excited wave in a non-linear medium.png|300px|Schematic view of the SHG conversion of an exciting wave in a non-linear medium with a non-zero second-order non-linear susceptibility]]

==History==
[[File:Electron asymmetric motion animation.gif|thumb|300px|An electron (purple) is being pushed side-to-side by a [[sinusoid]]ally oscillating force, i.e. the light's electric field. But because the electron is in an [[anharmonic]] [[potential energy]] environment (black curve), the electron motion is ''not'' sinusoidal. The three arrows show the [[Fourier series]] of the motion: The blue arrow corresponds to ordinary (linear) [[electric susceptibility|susceptibility]], the green arrow corresponds to second-harmonic generation, and the red arrow corresponds to [[optical rectification]].]]

Second-harmonic generation was first demonstrated by [[Peter Franken]], A. E. Hill, C. W. Peters, and [[Gabriel Weinreich|G. Weinreich]] at the [[University of Michigan]], Ann Arbor, in 1961.<ref name=peter1961 /> The demonstration was made possible by the invention of the [[laser]], which created the required high-intensity coherent light. They focused a [[ruby laser]] with a wavelength of 694 nm into a quartz sample. They sent the output light through a [[spectrometer]], recording the spectrum on [[photographic paper]], which indicated the production of light at 347 nm. Famously, when published in the journal ''Physical Review Letters'',<ref name=peter1961>{{cite journal |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118 |title=Generation of Optical Harmonics |year=1961 |last1=Franken |first1=P. |last2=Hill |first2=A. |last3=Peters |first3=C. |last4=Weinreich |first4=G. |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=7 |pages=118–119 |bibcode=1961PhRvL...7..118F |issue=4 |doi-access=free}}</ref> the copy editor mistook the dim spot (at 347 nm) on the photographic paper as a speck of dirt and removed it from the publication.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Haroche |first=Serge |title=Essay: Fifty Years of Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics in Physical Review Letters |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=October 17, 2008 |volume=101 |issue=16 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.160001 |bibcode=2008PhRvL.101p0001H |pmid=18999650 |article-number=160001}}</ref> The formulation of SHG was initially described by [[Nicolaas Bloembergen|N. Bloembergen]] and [[Peter Pershan|P. S. Pershan]] at Harvard in 1962.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bloembergen | first1 = N. | last2 = Pershan | first2 = P. S. | year = 1962 | title = Light Waves at Boundary of Nonlinear Media | url = https://dspace.library.uu.nl/bitstream/1874/7432/1/1962-bloembergen-ligtwaves.pdf | journal = Physical Review | volume = 128 | issue = 2 | pages = 606–622 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.128.606 |bibcode = 1962PhRv..128..606B | hdl = 1874/7432 }}</ref> In their extensive evaluation of [[Maxwell's equations]] at the planar interface between a linear and nonlinear medium, several rules for the interaction of light in non-linear media were elucidated.

==Types in crystals==

===Critical phase-matching===
[[File:TypeX SHG.png|thumb|Different types of second-harmonic generation phase-matching of a coherent light for strong conversion. The case of negative crystals (<math>n_o>n_e</math>) is considered, invert indices if positive crystal (<math>n_e>n_o</math>).]]
Second-harmonic generation occurs in three types for critical phase-matching,<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.rp-photonics.com/critical_phase_matching.html |title=Critical phase-matching |author=<!--Not stated--> |website= rp-photonics.com|access-date=2019-11-01 }}</ref> denoted 0, I and II. In ''Type 0 SHG,'' two photons having [[extraordinary polarization]] with respect to the crystal will combine to form a single photon with double the frequency/energy and extraordinary polarization. In ''Type I SHG,'' two photons having [[ordinary polarization]] with respect to the crystal will combine to form one photon with double the frequency and extraordinary polarization. In ''Type II SHG'', two photons having orthogonal polarizations will combine to form one photon with double the frequency and ordinary polarization. For a given crystal orientation, only one of these types of SHG occurs. In general, to utilize ''Type 0'' interactions, a [[quasi-phase-matching]] crystal type is required, such as [[periodically poled lithium niobate]] (PPLN).

===Non-critical phase-matching===
Since phase-matching processes simply match the optical indices at ω and 2ω, they can also be done by controlling temperature in birefringent crystals where the optical index is temperature-dependent. For instance, [[Lithium triborate|LBO]] presents a perfect phase-matching at 25 °C for a SHG excited at 1200 or 1400 nm,<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.rp-photonics.com/noncritical_phase_matching.html |title=Noncritical phase-matching |author=<!--Not stated--> |website= rp-photonics.com|access-date=2019-11-01 }}</ref> but needs to be elevated at 200 °C for SHG with the usual laser line of 1064 nm. It is called "non-critical" because it does not depend on the crystal orientation, unlike usual phase-matching.

==Surface second-harmonic generation==
[[Image:Second Harmonic Generation.svg|512px|thumb|right|Diagram of the second-harmonic generation process]]

Since media with [[inversion symmetry]] are forbidden from generating second-harmonic light via the leading-order electric dipole contribution (unlike [[Harmonic generation#Third-harmonic generation (THG)|third harmonic generation]]), surfaces and interfaces make interesting subjects for study with SHG. In fact, second-harmonic generation and sum frequency generation discriminate against signals from the bulk, implicitly labeling them as surface specific techniques. In 1982, [[Tony Heinz|T. F. Heinz]] and Y. R. Shen explicitly demonstrated for the first time that SHG could be used as a spectroscopic technique to probe molecular monolayers adsorbed to surfaces.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Heinz | first1 = T. F. | display-authors = etal   | year = 1982 | title = Spectroscopy of Molecular Monolayers by Resonant 2nd-Harmonic Generation | url = http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/3554s3wq| journal = Physical Review Letters | volume = 48 | issue = 7| pages = 478–81 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.48.478 | bibcode=1982PhRvL..48..478H}}</ref> Heinz and Shen adsorbed monolayers of laser dye [[rhodamine]] to a planar [[fused silica]] surface; the coated surface was then pumped by a nanosecond ultra-fast laser. SH light with characteristic spectra of the adsorbed molecule and its electronic transitions were measured as reflection from the surface and demonstrated a quadratic power dependence on the pump laser power.

In SHG surface spectroscopy, one focuses on measuring twice the incident frequency 2''ω'' given an incoming electric field <math>E(\omega)</math> in order to reveal information about a surface. Simply (for a more in-depth derivation see below), the induced second-harmonic dipole per unit volume, <math>P^{(2)}(2\omega)</math>, can be written as

: <math>E(2\omega) \propto P^{(2)}(2\omega) = \chi^{(2)} E(\omega) E(\omega)</math>

where <math>\chi^{(2)}</math> is known as the nonlinear susceptibility tensor and is a characteristic to the materials at the interface of study.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Shen | first1 = Y. R. | year = 1989 | title = Surface-Properties Probed by 2nd-Harmonic and Sum-Frequency Generation | url = https://zenodo.org/record/1233109| journal = Nature | volume = 337 | issue = 6207| pages = 519–25 | doi = 10.1038/337519a0 |bibcode = 1989Natur.337..519S | s2cid = 4233043 }}</ref> The generated <math>E(2\omega)</math> and corresponding <math>\chi^{(2)}</math> have been shown to reveal information about the orientation of molecules at a surface/interface, the interfacial analytical chemistry of surfaces, and chemical reactions at interfaces. SHG surface spectroscopy is also used extensively in the electrochemical characterization of materials, since the [[electric field]] at the interface between the electrode and electrolyte introduces an additional term that affects the interfacial inversion symmetry.

===From planar surfaces===
{{Main|Surface second harmonic generation}}
[[File:SHG phenol air-water.png|400px|thumb|A depiction of the second-harmonic generation setup for measuring the orientation of phenol at the air-water interface.]]
Early experiments in the field demonstrated second-harmonic generation from metal surfaces.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Brown | first1 = F. | last2 = Matsuoka | first2 = M. | year = 1969 | title = Effect of Adsorbed Surface Layers on Second-Harmonic Light from Silver | journal = Physical Review | volume = 185 | issue = 3| pages = 985–987 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.185.985 |bibcode = 1969PhRv..185..985B }}</ref> Eventually, SHG was used to probe the air-water interface, allowing for detailed information about molecular orientation and ordering at one of the most ubiquitous of surfaces.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Eisenthal | first1 = K. B. | year = 1992 | title = Equilibrium and Dynamic Processes at Interfaces by 2nd Harmonic and Sum Frequency Generation | journal = Annual Review of Physical Chemistry | volume = 43 | issue = 1| pages = 627–61 | doi = 10.1146/annurev.physchem.43.1.627 }}</ref> It can be shown that the specific elements of <math>\chi^{(2)}</math>:

: <math>\begin{align}
  \chi^{(2)}_{zzz} &= N_s \left\langle \cos^3(\theta) \right\rangle \alpha^{(2)}_{zzz} \\
  \chi^{(2)}_{xzx} &= \frac{1}{2} N_s \left\langle \cos(\theta) \sin^2(\theta) \right\rangle \alpha^{(2)}_{zzz}
\end{align}</math>

where ''N''<sub>''s''</sub> is the adsorbate density, ''θ'' is the angle that the molecular axis ''z'' makes with the surface normal ''Z'', and <math>\alpha^{(2)}_{zzz}</math> is the dominating element of the nonlinear polarizability of a molecule at an interface, allow one to determine&nbsp;''θ'', given laboratory coordinates {{nowrap|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}}.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Kemnitz | first1 = K. | display-authors = etal  | year = 1986 | title = The Phase of 2nd-Harmonic Light Generated at an Interface and Its Relation to Absolute Molecular-Orientation | journal = Chemical Physics Letters | volume = 131 | issue = 4–5| pages = 285–90 | doi = 10.1016/0009-2614(86)87152-4 |bibcode = 1986CPL...131..285K | citeseerx = 10.1.1.549.6666 | s2cid = 53476039 }}</ref> Using an interference SHG method to determine these elements of ''χ''(2), the first molecular orientation measurement showed that the hydroxyl group of phenol pointed downwards into the water at the air-water interface (as expected due to the potential of hydroxyl groups to form hydrogen bonds). Additionally SHG at planar surfaces has revealed differences in ''pK''<sup>''a''</sup> and rotational motions of molecules at interfaces.

===From non-planar surfaces===
[[File:SHG from small sphere.png|300px|thumbnail|Cartoon depicting ordered molecules at a small spherical surface. An ultrafast pump laser pumps light with frequency ω which generates light at 2ω from the locally non-centrosymmetric media.]]
Second-harmonic light can also be generated from surfaces that are "locally" planar, but may have inversion symmetry (centrosymmetric) on a larger scale. Specifically, recent theory has demonstrated that SHG from small spherical particles (micro- and nanometer scale) is allowed by proper treatment of [[Rayleigh scattering]] (scattering without a change in frequency from absorbed to emitted waves).<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Dadap | first1 = J. I. | last2 = Shan | first2 = J. | last3 = Heinz | first3 = T. F. | year = 2004 | title = Theory of Optical Second-Harmonic Generation from a Sphere of Centrosymmetric Material: Small-Particle Limit | journal = Journal of the Optical Society of America B | volume = 21 | issue = 7| pages = 1328–47 | doi = 10.1364/JOSAB.21.001328 |bibcode = 2004JOSAB..21.1328D }}</ref> At the surface of a small sphere, inversion symmetry is broken, allowing for SHG and other even order harmonics to occur.

For a colloidal system of microparticles at relatively low concentrations, the total SH signal <math>I^\text{total}_{2\omega}</math>, is given by:

: <math>I^\text{total}_{2\omega} \propto \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \left(E^{2\omega}_j\right)^2 = n\left(E^{2\omega}\right)^2 = nI_{2\omega}</math>

where <math>E^{2\omega}_j</math> is the SH electric field generated by the ''j''th particle, and ''n'' is the density of particles.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Eisenthal | first1 = K. B. | year = 2006 | title = Second Harmonic Spectroscopy of Aqueous Nano- and Microparticle Interfaces | journal = Chemical Reviews | volume = 106 | issue = 4| pages = 1462–77 | doi = 10.1021/cr0403685 | pmid=16608187}}</ref> The SH light generated from each particle is [[Coherence (physics)|coherent]], but adds incoherently to the SH light generated by others (as long as density is low enough). Thus, SH light is only generated from the interfaces of the spheres and their environment and is independent of particle-particle interactions. It has also been shown that the second-harmonic electric field <math>E(2\omega)</math> scales with the radius of the particle cubed, a<sup>3</sup>.

Besides spheres, other small particles like rods have been studied similarly by SHG.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Chan | first1 = S. W. | display-authors = etal   | year = 2006 | title = Second Harmonic Generation in Zinc Oxide Nanorods | journal = Applied Physics B: Lasers and Optics | volume = 84 | issue = 1–2| pages = 351–55 | doi = 10.1007/s00340-006-2292-0 |bibcode = 2006ApPhB..84..351C | s2cid = 120094124 }}</ref> Both immobilized and colloidal systems of small particles can be investigated. Recent experiments using second-harmonic generation of non-planar systems include transport kinetics across living cell membranes<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Zeng | first1 = Jia | display-authors = etal   | year = 2013 | title = Time-Resolved Molecular Transport across Living Cell Membranes | journal = Biophysical Journal | volume = 104 | issue = 1| pages = 139–45 | doi = 10.1016/j.bpj.2012.11.3814 | pmid=23332066 | pmc=3540258| bibcode = 2013BpJ...104..139Z }}</ref> and demonstrations of SHG in complex [[nanomaterials]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Fan | first1 = W. | display-authors = etal   | year = 2006 | title = Second Harmonic Generation from a Nanopatterned Isotropic Nonlinear Material | journal = Nano Letters | volume = 6 | issue = 5| pages = 1027–30 | doi = 10.1021/nl0604457 |bibcode = 2006NanoL...6.1027F | citeseerx = 10.1.1.172.8506 }}</ref>

==Radiation pattern==
[[File:SHG radiation pattern from interfaces or not.png|thumb|300px|left|SHG radiation pattern excited with a Gaussian beam, in a homogeneous medium (A), or at an interface between opposite polarities that is parallel to the propagation (B). Only the forward SHG is represented.]]

The SHG [[radiation pattern]] generated by an exciting Gaussian beam also has a (homogeneous) 2D Gaussian profile if the nonlinear medium being excited is homogeneous (A). However, if the exciting beam is positioned at an interface between opposite polarities (± boundary, ''B'') that is parallel to the beam propagation (see figure), the SHG will be split into two lobes whose amplitudes have opposite sign, i.e. are <math>\pi</math> phase-shifted.
<ref name="MoreauxSandre2001">{{cite journal|last1=Moreaux|first1=Laurent|last2=Sandre|first2=Olivier|last3=Charpak|first3=Serge|last4=Blanchard-Desce|first4=Mireille|last5=Mertz|first5=Jerome|title=Coherent Scattering in Multi-Harmonic Light Microscopy|journal=Biophysical Journal|volume=80|issue=3|year=2001|pages=1568–1574|issn=0006-3495|doi=10.1016/S0006-3495(01)76129-2|pmid=11222317|pmc=1301348|bibcode=2001BpJ....80.1568M}}</ref>

These boundaries can be found in the [[sarcomere]]s of [[muscle]]s (protein = [[myosin]]), for instance. Note that we have considered here only the forward generation.

{{See also|Second-harmonic imaging microscopy#Forward over backward SHG}}

Additionally, the SHG [[Nonlinear optics#Phase matching|phase-matching]] can result in <math>\vec k_{2\omega} = -2\vec k_\omega</math>: some SHG is also emitted in backward (epi direction). When the [[Nonlinear optics#Phase matching|phase-matching]] is not fulfilled, as in [[biological tissue]]s, the backward signal comes from a sufficiently high phase-mismatch which allow a small backward contribution to compensate for it.<ref name="CampagnolaLoew2003">{{cite journal|title=Second-harmonic imaging microscopy for visualizing biomolecular arrays in cells, tissues and organisms|last1=Campagnola|first1=Paul J|last2=Loew|first2=Leslie M|journal=Nature Biotechnology|volume=21|pages=1356–1360<!--endif p.totales-->|year=2003|issue=11|issn=1087-0156|doi=10.1038/nbt894|pmid=14595363|s2cid=18701570}}</ref> Unlike fluorescence, the spatial coherence of the process constrain it to emit only in those two directions, where the coherence length in the backwards direction is always much smaller than in the forwards, meaning there is always more forward than backward SHG signal.<ref name="LaCombNadiarnykh2008">{{cite journal|last1=LaComb|first1=Ronald|last2=Nadiarnykh|first2=Oleg|last3=Townsend|first3=Sallie S.|last4=Campagnola|first4=Paul J.|title=Phase matching considerations in second harmonic generation from tissues: Effects on emission directionality, conversion efficiency and observed morphology|journal=Optics Communications|volume=281|issue=7|year=2008|pages=1823–1832|issn=0030-4018|doi=10.1016/j.optcom.2007.10.040|pmid=19343083|pmc=2390911|bibcode=2008OptCo.281.1823L}}</ref>

[[File:FB diagram stacking.png|thumb|500px|right|SHG radiation pattern in forward (F) and backward (B) from different dipoles arangment: (a) single dipoles, thus ''F''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''B'' ; (b) a small stack of dipoles, ''F''&nbsp;>&nbsp;''B'' ; (c) a large stack of dipoles, ''F''&nbsp;>>&nbsp;''B'' ; (d) the Gouy phase-shift cancels the SHGs, ''F''&nbsp;&&nbsp;''B'' weak]]
The forward (''F'') to backward (''B'') ratio is dependent on the arrangement of the different dipoles (green in figure) that are being excited. With only one dipole ((a) in the figure), ''F''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''B'', but ''F'' becomes higher than ''B'' when more dipoles are stacked along the propagation direction (b and c). However, the [[Gaussian beam#Gouy phase|Gouy phase-shift]] of the [[Gaussian beam]] will imply a <math>\pi</math> phase-shift between the SHGs generated at the edges of the focal volume, and can thus result in destructive interferences (zero signal) if there are dipoles at these edges having the same orientation (case (d) in the figure).

The forward (''F'') to backward (''B'') ratio is dependent on the arrangement of the different dipoles (green in figure) that are being excited. With only one dipole ((a) in the figure), ''F''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''B'', but ''F'' becomes higher than ''B'' when more dipoles are stacked along the propagation direction (b and c). However, the [[Gaussian beam#Gouy phase|Gouy phase-shift]] of the [[Gaussian beam]] will imply a <math>\pi</math> phase-shift between the SHGs generated at the edges of the focal volume, and can thus result in destructive interferences (zero signal) if there are dipoles at these edges having the same orientation (case (d) in the figure).

==Applications==

===Green lasers===
Second-harmonic generation is used by the laser industry to make green 532&nbsp;nm lasers from a 1064&nbsp;nm source. The 1064&nbsp;nm light is fed through a bulk nonlinear crystal (typically made of  [[potassium dihydrogen phosphate|KDP]] or [[Potassium titanyl phosphate|KTP]]). In high-quality diode lasers the crystal is coated on the output side with an infrared filter to prevent leakage of intense 1064&nbsp;nm or 808&nbsp;nm infrared light into the beam. Both of these wavelengths are invisible and do not trigger the defensive "blink-reflex" reaction in the eye and can therefore be a special hazard to human eyes. Furthermore, some [[laser safety]] eyewear intended for argon or other green lasers may filter out the green component (giving a false sense of safety), but transmit the infrared. Nevertheless, some "green [[laser pointer]]" products have become available on the market which omit the expensive infrared filter, often without warning.<ref>[http://www.wickedlasers.com/laser-tech/WhyisIRbad.html A warning about IR in green cheap green laser pointers]</ref>

===Ultra-short pulse measurement===

Second-harmonic generation is also used for measuring ultra-short pulse widths with [[autocorrelator]]s. Characterizing an [[ultrashort pulse]] (like measuring its temporal width) cannot be done directly with electronics only, as the time-scale is below 1ps (<math>10^{-12}</math>sec). One therefore needs to use the pulse itself, often through an autocorrelation function. Since SHG has the advantage of mixing two input fields to generate the harmonic field, it is a good candidate for performing such pulse measurements. [[Optical autocorrelation]], in its [[Optical autocorrelation#Intensity autocorrelation|intensity]] or fringe-resolved ([[Optical autocorrelation#Interferometric autocorrelation|interferometric]]) versions, uses SHG,<ref name="TrebinoZeek2000">{{cite book|last1=Trebino|first1=Rick|last2=Zeek|first2=Erik|chapter=Chap4, The Autocorrelation, the Spectrum, and Phase Retrieval|title=Frequency-Resolved Optical Gating: The Measurement of Ultrashort Laser Pulses|url=https://archive.org/details/frequencyresolve00treb|url-access=limited|year=2000|pages=[https://archive.org/details/frequencyresolve00treb/page/n74 61]–99|publisher=Springer|doi=10.1007/978-1-4615-1181-6_4|isbn=978-1-4615-1181-6}}</ref> unlike linear [[Optical autocorrelation#Field autocorrelation|field autocorrelation]]. Also, most versions of [[Frequency-resolved optical gating|FROG]] (called SHG-FROG) use SHG to mix the delayed fields.<ref name="Trebino2003">{{cite book|last1=Trebino|first1=Rick|chapter=Chap5, FROG|title=Frequency-Resolved Optical Gating: The Measurement of Ultrashort Laser Pulses|url=https://archive.org/details/frequencyresolve00treb|url-access=limited|year=2003|pages=[https://archive.org/details/frequencyresolve00treb/page/n74 61]–99|doi=10.1007/978-1-4615-1181-6_5|isbn=978-1-4615-1181-6|publisher=Springer}}</ref>

===Second-harmonic generation microscopy===
{{Main|Second-harmonic imaging microscopy}}
In biological and medical science, the effect of second-harmonic generation is used for high-resolution optical microscopy. Because of the non-zero second-harmonic coefficient, only non-centrosymmetric structures are capable of emitting SHG light.  One such structure is collagen, which is found in most load-bearing tissues. Using a short-pulse laser such as a [[femtosecond laser]] and a set of appropriate filters the excitation light can be easily separated from the emitted, frequency-doubled SHG signal. This allows for very high axial and lateral resolution comparable to that of [[confocal microscopy]] without having to use pinholes. SHG microscopy has been used for studies of the [[cornea]]<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1364/OPEX.13.005791|url=http://www.opticsexpress.org/viewmedia.cfm?id=85235&seq=0|pmid=19498583|year=2005|last1=Han|first1=M|last2=Giese|first2=G|last3=Bille|first3=J|title=Second harmonic generation imaging of collagen fibrils in cornea and sclera|volume=13|issue=15|pages=5791–7|journal=Optics Express|bibcode = 2005OExpr..13.5791H |doi-access=free}}</ref> and [[lamina cribrosa sclerae]],<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1117/1.2717540|title=Application of second harmonic imaging microscopy to assess structural changes in optic nerve head structure ex vivo|pmid=17477744|year=2007|last1=Brown|first1=Donald J.|last2=Morishige|first2=Naoyuki|last3=Neekhra|first3=Aneesh|last4=Minckler|first4=Don S.|last5=Jester|first5=James V.|journal=Journal of Biomedical Optics|volume=12|issue=2|page=024029 |bibcode = 2007JBO....12b4029B |s2cid=33236022|doi-access=free}}</ref> both of which consist primarily of collagen. Second-harmonic generation can be produced by several non-centrosymmetric organic dyes; however, most of the organic dyes also generate collateral fluorescence along with second-harmonic generation signals.<ref name="Khadria et al.2018">{{cite journal|vauthors=Khadria A, Fleischhauer J, Boczarow I, Wilkinson JD, Kohl MM, Anderson HL|title= Porphyrin Dyes for Nonlinear Optical Imaging of Live Cells |journal=iScience |pages= 153–163 |year=2018|doi=10.1016/j.isci.2018.05.015 |pmid= 30240737 |pmc= 6147020 |volume=4|bibcode= 2018iSci....4..153K }}</ref> Until now, only two classes of organic dyes have been shown which do not produce any collateral fluorescence and works purely on second-harmonic generation.<ref name="Khadria et al.2018"/><ref name="Nuriya et al.2016">{{cite journal|vauthors=Nuriya M, Fukushima S, Momotake A, Shinotsuka T, Yasui M, Arai T|title= Multimodal two-photon imaging using a second-harmonic generation-specific dye |journal=Nature Communications |article-number= 11557  |year=2016|doi= 10.1038/ncomms11557 |doi-access= free|pmid= 27156702 |pmc= 4865818 |volume=7|bibcode=2016NatCo...711557N}}</ref> Recently, using two-photon excited fluorescence and second-harmonic generation-based microscopy, a group of Oxford University researchers showed that organic porphyrin-type molecules can have different transition dipole moments for two-photon fluorescence and second-harmonic generation,<ref name="Khadria et al.2017">{{cite journal|vauthors=Khadria A, Coene Y, Gawel P, Roche C, Clays K, Anderson HL|title= Push–pull pyropheophorbides for nonlinear optical imaging |journal=Organic and Biomolecular Chemistry |pages= 947–956 |year=2017|doi=10.1039/C6OB02319C |pmid= 28054076 |volume=15|issue= 4 |s2cid= 3540505 |url= https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:e885d41b-c569-4239-9f7d-25cf640de228 }}</ref> which are otherwise thought to occur from the same transition dipole moment.<ref name="Reeve et al._2017">{{cite journal|vauthors=Reeve JE, Corbett AD, Boczarow I, Wilson T, Bayley H, Anderson HL|title= Probing the Orientational Distribution of Dyes in Membranes through Multiphoton Microscopy |journal=Biophysical Journal |pages= 907–917 |year=2012|doi=10.1016/j.bpj.2012.08.003 |pmid= 23009840 |pmc= 3433607 |volume=103|issue= 5 |bibcode=2012BpJ...103..907R}}</ref>

Second-harmonic generation microscopy is also used in material science, for instance to characterize nanostructured materials.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1021/la302485c|pmid=22889193|year=2012|author1-link=Ventsislav K. Valev|last1=Valev|first1=V. K.|title=Characterization of nanostructured plasmonic surfaces with second harmonic generation|volume=28|issue=44|pages=15454–15471|journal=Langmuir}}</ref>

===Characterization of crystalline materials===
Second harmonic generation is also relevant to characterize organic or inorganic crystals<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Simon|first1=Florent|last2=Clevers|first2=Simon|last3=Dupray|first3=Valérie|last4=Coquerel|first4=Gérard|date=2015|title=Relevance of the Second Harmonic Generation to Characterize Crystalline Samples|journal=Chemical Engineering & Technology|language=en|volume=38|issue=6|pages=971–983|doi=10.1002/ceat.201400756}}</ref> since is one of the most discriminant and rapid technique to detect [[Non-centrosymmetric|non-centrosymmetry]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Abrahams|first=S. C.|date=1972-04-01|title=Letter to the Editor|url=http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0021889872009045|journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography|volume=5|issue=2|page=143|doi=10.1107/S0021889872009045|issn=0021-8898|doi-access=free|bibcode=1972JApCr...5..143A }}</ref> In addition, this technique can be used on [[single crystal]] as well as on powdered samples. One should recall that SHG is only possible (from the bulk) in non-centrosymmetric (NC) [[crystal]]s. The part of non-centroysmmetric crystals in nature is much lower than centrosymmetric crystals (circa 22% of the Cambridge structural database<ref>{{Cite web|title=CCDC Statistics|url=https://www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk/support-and-resources/ccdcresources/}}</ref>), but the frequency of NC crystals increases by a lot in pharmaceutical, biological and electronic fields because of the particular properties of these crystals ([[piezoelectricity]], [[pyroelectricity]], polar phases, [[Chirality (chemistry)|chirality]], etc.).

In 1968<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kurtz|first1=S. K.|last2=Perry|first2=T. T.|date=1968|title=A Powder Technique for the Evaluation of Nonlinear Optical Materials|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|language=en|volume=39|issue=8|pages=3798–3813|doi=10.1063/1.1656857|bibcode=1968JAP....39.3798K|issn=0021-8979|doi-access=free}}</ref> (7 years after the first experimental evidence of SHG on single crystal<ref name="peter1961" />), Kurtz and Perry started to develop a SHG analyzer to rapidly detect the presence or not of inversion center in powdered crystalline samples. The detection of a SHG signal has been shown to be reliable and sensitive test for the detection of crystalline non-centrosymmetry with the confidence level higher than 99%. It is a relevant tool to resolve space group ambiguities that can arise from Friedel's law in single-crystal X-ray diffraction.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dougherty|first1=J. P.|last2=Kurtz|first2=S. K.|date=1976-04-01|title=A second harmonic analyzer for the detection of non-centrosymmetry|url=http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0021889876010789|journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography|volume=9|issue=2|pages=145–158|doi=10.1107/S0021889876010789|bibcode=1976JApCr...9..145D |issn=0021-8898|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Furthermore, the method is referenced in the International Tables for Crystallography and is described as a "powerful method of testing crystalline materials for the absence of a symmetry center."<ref>{{Cite book|title=International tables for crystallography.|date=2002|publisher=Kluwer|others=International Union of Crystallography.|isbn=0-7923-6591-7|edition=5th rev.|location=Dordrecht|oclc=48400542}}</ref>

One possible application is also to rapidly discriminate chiral phases such as [[Racemic mixture|conglomerate]] that are of particular interest for pharmaceutical industries.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Galland|first1=Arnaud|last2=Dupray|first2=Valerie|last3=Berton|first3=Benjamin|last4=Morin-Grognet|first4=Sandrine|last5=Sanselme|first5=Morgane|last6=Atmani|first6=Hassan|last7=Coquerel|first7=Gérard|date=2009-06-03|title=Spotting Conglomerates by Second Harmonic Generation|journal=Crystal Growth & Design|language=en|volume=9|issue=6|pages=2713–2718|doi=10.1021/cg801356m|issn=1528-7483}}</ref> It could also be used as a technique to probe the structural purity of material if one of the impurities is NC reaching a detection threshold as low as 1 ppm<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clevers|first1=S.|last2=Simon|first2=F.|last3=Dupray|first3=V.|last4=Coquerel|first4=G.|date=2013|title=Temperature resolved second harmonic generation to probe the structural purity of m-hydroxybenzoic acid|journal=Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry|language=en|volume=112|issue=1|pages=271–277|doi=10.1007/s10973-012-2763-y|s2cid=138727698|issn=1388-6150}}</ref> using Kurtz–Perry apparatus up to one part in 10 billion by volume using a SHG microscope.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wanapun|first1=Duangporn|last2=Kestur|first2=Umesh S.|last3=Kissick|first3=David J.|last4=Simpson|first4=Garth J.|last5=Taylor|first5=Lynne S.|date=2010|title=Selective Detection and Quantitation of Organic Molecule Crystallization by Second Harmonic Generation Microscopy|journal=Analytical Chemistry|language=en|volume=82|issue=13|pages=5425–5432|doi=10.1021/ac100564f|pmid=20515064|issn=0003-2700}}</ref>

Due to the high sensitivity of the technique, it can be a helpful tool in the accurate determination of [[phase diagram]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yuan|first1=Lina|last2=Clevers|first2=Simon|last3=Couvrat|first3=Nicolas|last4=Cartigny|first4=Yohann|last5=Dupray|first5=Valérie|last6=Coquerel|first6=Gérard|date=2016|title=Precise Urea/Water Eutectic Composition by Temperature-Resolved Second Harmonic Generation|journal=Chemical Engineering & Technology|language=en|volume=39|issue=7|pages=1326–1332|doi=10.1002/ceat.201600032}}</ref> and can also be used to monitor phase transitions ([[Polymorphism (materials science)|polymorphic]] transition, dehydration, ...) when at least one of the phases is NC.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Yuan|first1=Lina|last2=Clevers|first2=Simon|last3=Burel|first3=Antoine|last4=Negrier|first4=Philippe|last5=Barrio|first5=Maria del|last6=Ben Hassine|first6=Bacem|last7=Mondieig|first7=Denise|last8=Dupray|first8=Valérie|last9=Tamarit|first9=Josep Ll.|last10=Coquerel|first10=Gérard|date=2017-06-07|title=New Intermediate Polymorph of 1-Fluoro-adamantane and Its Second-Order-like Transition toward the Low Temperature Phase|journal=Crystal Growth & Design|language=en|volume=17|issue=6|pages=3395–3401|doi=10.1021/acs.cgd.7b00353|hdl=2117/106369|issn=1528-7483|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clevers|first1=S.|last2=Rougeot|first2=C.|last3=Simon|first3=F.|last4=Sanselme|first4=M.|last5=Dupray|first5=V.|last6=Coquerel|first6=G.|date=2014|title=Detection of order–disorder transition in organic solids by using temperature resolved second harmonic generation (TR-SHG)|journal=Journal of Molecular Structure|language=en|volume=1078|pages=61–67|doi=10.1016/j.molstruc.2014.04.007|bibcode=2014JMoSt1078...61C}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clevers|first1=Simon|last2=Simon|first2=Florent|last3=Sanselme|first3=Morgane|last4=Dupray|first4=Valerie|last5=Coquerel|first5=Gerard|date=2013-08-07|title=Monotropic Transition Mechanism of m -Hydroxybenzoic Acid Investigated by Temperature-Resolved Second Harmonic Generation|journal=Crystal Growth & Design|language=en|volume=13|issue=8|pages=3697–3704|doi=10.1021/cg400712s|issn=1528-7483}}</ref>

==Theoretical derivation (plane wave)==

===At low conversion===
The simplest case for analysis of second-harmonic generation is a [[plane wave]] of amplitude ''E''(''ω'') traveling in a nonlinear medium in the direction of its [[wave vector|''k'' vector]]. A polarization is generated at the second-harmonic frequency:<ref name="Boyd 2008">{{Cite book|title= Nonlinear Optics, 3rd edition|last= Boyd|first= R.W. | year=2008|publisher= Academic Press|isbn=978-0-12-121680-1|url=https://archive.org/details/nonlinearoptics0000boyd}}</ref>

:<math>P(2\omega) = \varepsilon_0 \chi^{(2)} E^2(\omega) = 2\varepsilon_0 d_\text{eff}(2\omega; \omega, \omega) E^2(\omega),\,</math>

where <math>d_\text{eff}</math> is the effective nonlinear optical coefficient which is dependent on specific components of <math>\chi^{(2)}</math> that are involved in this particular interaction. The wave equation at 2ω (assuming negligible loss and asserting the [[slowly varying envelope approximation]]) is

:<math>\frac{\partial E(2\omega)}{\partial z} = -\frac{i\omega}{n_{2\omega}c} d_\text{eff} E^2(\omega)e^{i \, \Delta k \, z}</math>

where <math>\Delta k = k(2\omega) - 2k(\omega)</math>.

At low conversion efficiency (''E''(2''ω'') ≪ ''E''(''ω'')) the amplitude <math>E(\omega)</math> remains essentially constant over the interaction length, <math>\ell</math>. Then, with the boundary condition <math>E(2\omega, z = 0) = 0</math> we obtain

: <math>E(2\omega, z = \ell) =
  -\frac{i\omega d_\text{eff}}{n_{2\omega}c} E^2(\omega) \int_0^\ell e^{i\,\Delta k \, z} \, dz =
  -\frac{i\omega d_\text{eff}}{n_{2\omega}c} E^2(\omega) \ell\, \frac{\sin\left(\frac{1}{2}\,\Delta k \, \ell\right)}{\frac{1}{2}\,\Delta k\, \ell} e^{\frac{i}{2} \, \Delta k\, \ell}
</math>

In terms of the optical intensity, <math>I = n/2\sqrt{\varepsilon_0/\mu_0}|E|^2</math>, this is,

: <math>I(2\omega,\ell) = \frac{2\omega^2 d^2_\text{eff} \ell^2}{n_{2\omega} n_\omega^2 c^3 \varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{\sin\left(\frac{1}{2} \,\Delta k \, \ell\right)}{\frac{1}{2} \,\Delta k\, \ell}\right)^2 I^2(\omega)</math>

This intensity is maximized for the [[Nonlinear optics#Phase matching|phase-matched]] condition Δ''k'' = 0. If the process is not phase matched, the driving polarization at ''ω'' goes in and out of phase with generated wave ''E''(2''ω'') and conversion oscillates as sin(Δ''kℓ''/2). The coherence length is defined as <math>\ell_c = \frac{\pi}{\Delta k}</math>. It does not pay to use a nonlinear crystal much longer than the coherence length. ([[Periodic poling]] and [[quasi-phase-matching]] provide another approach to this problem.)

===With depletion===
[[File:Frequency doubling with perfect pase matching.gif|400px|thumb|right|Diagram of second-harmonic generation with perfect phase matching <math>\Delta k = 0</math>.]]
[[File:Frequency doubling with imperfect phase matching.gif|400px|thumb|right|Diagram of second-harmonic generation with an imperfect phase matching <math>\Delta k \neq 0</math>. In this case energy flows forth and back from the pump to the frequency doubled signal, and having a thick crystal can lead to a smaller amount of SHG produced.]]

When the conversion to 2nd harmonic becomes significant it becomes necessary to include depletion of the fundamental. The energy conversion states that all the involved fields verify the [[Manley–Rowe relations]]. One then has the coupled equations:<ref>{{Cite book|title= Applied Nonlinear Optics|last1= Zernike|first1= Frits|last2= Midwinter |first2= John E. |year=1973|isbn=0-486-45360-X|publisher=John Wiley & Sons Inc.|url=https://archive.org/details/AppliedNonlinearOptics/page/n61}}</ref>

: <math>\begin{align}
  \frac{\partial E(2\omega)}{\partial z} &= -\frac{i\omega}{n_{2\omega}c} d_\text{eff} E^2(\omega) e^{i\,\Delta k \, z}, \\[5pt]
   \frac{\partial E(\omega)}{\partial z} &= -\frac{i\omega}{n_{\omega}c} d_\text{eff}^* E(2\omega) E^*(\omega)e^{-i\,\Delta k \, z},
\end{align}</math>

where <math>*</math> denotes the complex conjugate. For simplicity, assume phase matched generation (<math>\Delta k = 0</math>). Then, energy conservation requires that

: <math>
   n_{2\omega} \left[E^*(2\omega)\frac{\partial E(2\omega)}{\partial z} + \text{c.c.} \right] =
  -n_\omega \left[E(\omega)\frac{\partial E^*(\omega)}{\partial z} + \text{c.c.} \right]
</math>

where <math>\text{c.c.}</math> is the complex conjugate of the other term, or

: <math>n_{2\omega} \left|E(2\omega)\right|^2 + n_\omega|E(\omega)|^2 = n_{2\omega} E_0^2. </math>

[[File:Phase-matched SHG with source depletion.png|thumb|300px|Phase-matched SHG with source depletion (blue), and corresponding excitation (orange). ''L'' is the interaction length (''ℓ'' in the text).]]

Now we solve the equations with the premise
: <math>\begin{align}
   E(\omega) &= \left|E(\omega)\right| e^{i\varphi(\omega)} \\
  E(2\omega) &= \left|E(2\omega)\right| e^{i\varphi(2\omega)}
\end{align}</math>

and obtain
: <math>\frac{d\left|E(2\omega)\right|}{dz} = - \frac{i\omega d_\text{eff}}{n_\omega c}\left[E_0^2 - \left|E(2\omega)\right|^2\right] e^{2i\varphi(\omega) - i\varphi(2\omega)}</math>

which leads to
: <math>\int_0^{\left|E(2\omega)\right|\ell} \frac{d\left|E(2\omega)\right|}{E_0^2 - \left|E(2\omega)\right|^2} = -\int_0^\ell \frac{i\omega d_\text{eff}}{n_\omega c} e^{2i\varphi(\omega) - i\varphi(2\omega)} \, dz. </math>

Using
: <math>\int \frac{dx}{a^2 - x^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tanh^{-1} \frac{x}{a}</math>

we get
: <math> \left|E(2\omega)\right|_{z=\ell} = E_0\tanh \left(\frac{-iE_0\ell\omega d_\text{eff}}{n_\omega c} e^{2i\varphi(\omega) - i\varphi(2\omega)} \right). </math>

If we assume a real <math>d_\text{eff}</math>, the relative phases for real harmonic growth must be such that <math>e^{2i\varphi(\omega) - i\varphi(2\omega)} = i</math>. Then
: <math>I(2\omega, \ell) = I(\omega, 0) \tanh^2\left(\frac{E_0\omega d_\text{eff} \ell}{n_\omega c}\right) </math>

or
: <math>I(2\omega, \ell) = I(\omega,0)\tanh^2 (\Gamma \ell),</math>

where <math>\Gamma = \omega d_\text{eff} E_0/nc</math>. From <math>I(2\omega, \ell) + I(\omega,\ell) = I(\omega, 0)</math>, it also follows that
: <math>I(\omega, \ell) = I(\omega, 0) \operatorname{sech}^2(\Gamma \ell).</math>

==Theoretical expression with Gaussian beams==
The excitation wave is assumed to be a [[Gaussian beam]], of amplitude:
<math> A_1 = A_0 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\frac{z_R}{iq(z)} \exp \left( i k_1 \frac{x^2+y^2}{2q(z)} \right)</math>

with <math> q(z) = z-iz_R </math>, <math>z</math> the direction of propagation, <math>z_R</math> the Rayleigh range, <math>{k}_{1}</math> the [[wave vector]].

Each wave verifies the [[wave equation]]

: <math>\left[ \frac{\partial} {\partial x^2} +\frac\partial {\partial y^2} +2i k_1  \frac\partial{\partial z} \right] A(x,y,z;k_1) = \begin{cases}
   0  & \text{for the fundamental}, \\
   \frac{\omega_n^2 c^2}{\chi^{(n)}} A(x,y,z;k_1) e^{i\,\Delta k\, z} & \text{for } n\text{-th harmonic}.
\end{cases}
</math>

where <math>\Delta k = k_n - k_1</math>.

===With phase-matching===
It can be shown that:
<math> A_n =-i\frac{\omega_n}{2n_{n\omega}c}{\left( A_0 \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \right)^n} z_R^2 \int_{-\infty }^z \frac{\chi^{(n)}(u)}{q(u)^2} \, du \exp \left( ik_n \frac{x^2+y^2}{2q(z)} \right)</math>

(a [[Gaussian]]), is a solution of the equation (''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 for SHG).

===No phase-matching===
[[File:Intensity SHG, phase-matched or not.png|thumb|300px|Intensity SHG, phase-matched or not. The medium width is supposed to be much higher than ''z'', the Rayleigh range at 20&nbsp;μm, excitation wavelength of 0.8&nbsp;μm, and optical index of 2.2.]]
A non-perfect [[Nonlinear optics#Phase matching|phase-matching]] is a more realistic condition in practice, especially in biological samples. The paraxial approximation is however supposed still valid: <math>k_n = nk_1</math>, and in the harmonic expression, <math>\chi^{(n)}(z)</math> is now <math>\chi^{(n)}(z)e^{i\,\Delta k \, z}</math>.

In the special case of SHG (''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2), in a medium of length ''L'' and a focus position <math>z_0</math>, the intensity writes:<ref name="StollerCelliers2003">{{cite journal|last1=Stoller|first1=Patrick|last2=Celliers|first2=Peter M.|last3=Reiser|first3=Karen M.|last4=Rubenchik|first4=Alexander M.|title=Quantitative second-harmonic generation microscopy in collagen|journal=Applied Optics|volume=42|issue=25|year=2003|pages=5209–19|issn=0003-6935|doi=10.1364/AO.42.005209|pmid=12962402|bibcode=2003ApOpt..42.5209S}}</ref>

: <math> I_{2\omega} = \frac{2\omega^2 d_{\text{eff}}^2}{\pi c^3 \varepsilon_0 w_0^2 n_{2\omega} n_\omega^2} I_\omega^2 \left(  \int_{z_0}^{z_0+L} \frac{e^{i\,\Delta k \, z}}{1+iz/z_R} \right )^2 \, dz. </math>

where <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]] in [[vacuum]], <math>\varepsilon_0</math> the vacuum [[Vacuum permittivity|permittivity]], <math>n_{n\omega}</math> the [[Refractive index|optical index]] of the medium at <math>n\omega</math> and <math>w_0</math> the [[Gaussian beam#Beam waist|waist]] size of excitation.

Thus, the SHG intensity quickly decays in the bulk (<math>0 < z_0 < L </math>), due to the [[Gaussian beam#Gouy phase|Gouy phase-shift]] of the Gaussian beam.

In conformity with experiments, the SHG signal vanishes in the bulk (if the medium thickness is too large), and the SHG must be generated at the surface of the material: the conversion therefore does not strictly scales with the square of the number of scatterers, contrary to what the plane wave model indicates. Interestingly, the signal also vanishes in bulk for [[Harmonic generation|higher orders]], like THG.

==Materials used==
Materials capable of generating a second harmonic are crystals without inversion symmetry, except crystals with [[Crystallographic point group|point group]] 432. This eliminates water and glass.<ref name="Boyd 2008"/> 

Notably, filamentous biological proteins with a cylindrical symmetric such as [[collagen]], [[tubulin]] or [[myosin]], but also certain [[carbohydrates]] (such as [[starch]] or [[cellulose]]) are also quite good converters of SHG (fundamental in the near infrared).<ref>{{cite book |title=Second Harmonic Generation Imaging |edition=2nd |surname1=Pavone |first1=Francesco S. |surname2=Campagnola |first2=Paul J. |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-4398-4914-9 |publisher=CRC Taylor & Francis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EiTOBQAAQBAJ&q=Second+Harmonic+Generation+Imaging+Pavone+Francesco}}</ref>

Examples of [[crystal]]s used with for SHG conversion:
* Fundamental excitation at 600–1500&nbsp;nm:<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newlightphotonics.com/Nonlinear-Optical-Crystals/BiBO-Crystals |title=BiBO Crystals |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=newlightphotonics.com |access-date=2019-11-01 }}</ref> BiBO (BiB<sub>3</sub>O<sub>6</sub>)
* Fundamental excitation at 570–4000&nbsp;nm:<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.shalomeo.com/product/laser-components/nonlinear-crystals/liio3-crystals-117.html |title=LiIO<sub>3</sub> crystals – Lithium Iodate Crystal |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=shalomeo.com |access-date=2019-11-01 }}</ref> [[lithium iodate]] LiIO<sub>3</sub>.
* Fundamental excitation at 800–1100&nbsp;nm, often 860 or 980&nbsp;nm:<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.laser-crylink.com/laser-products/nonlinear-crystal/knbo3/ |title=KNbO<sub>3</sub> |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=laser-crylink.com |access-date=2019-11-01 }}</ref> [[potassium niobate]] KNbO<sub>3</sub>.
* Fundamental excitation at 410–2000&nbsp;nm: [[Barium borate|BBO]] (β-BaB<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newlightphotonics.com/Nonlinear-Optical-Crystals/BBO-Crystals |title=BBO Crystals |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=newlightphotonics.com |access-date=2019-11-01 }}</ref>
* Fundamental excitation at 984–3400&nbsp;nm: [[potassium titanyl phosphate|KTP]] (KTiOPO<sub>4</sub>) or KTA.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://unitedcrystals.com/KTPProp.html |title=KTP Crystals |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=unitedcrystals.com |access-date=2019-11-01 }}</ref>
* Fundamental excitation at ~1000–2000&nbsp;nm: periodically poled crystals, like [[Lithium niobate#Periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN)|PPLN]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/s003400100623 |title=Fabrication of periodically poled lithium tantalate for UV generation with diode lasers |journal=Applied Physics B |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=111–114 |year=2001 |last1=Meyn |first1=J.-P. |last2=Laue |first2=C. |last3=Knappe |first3=R. |last4=Wallenstein |first4=R. |last5=Fejer |first5=M. M. |bibcode=2001ApPhB..73..111M |s2cid=119763435}}</ref>

For common types of [[diode-pumped solid state]] lasers with input wavelengths:
* 1064&nbsp;nm: [[monopotassium phosphate]] KDP (KH<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>), [[lithium triborate]] (LiB<sub>3</sub>O<sub>5</sub>), CsLiB<sub>6</sub>O<sub>10</sub> and [[barium borate]] BBO(β-BaB<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>).
* 1319&nbsp;nm: KNbO<sub>3</sub>, [[Barium borate|BBO]] (β-BaB<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>), [[monopotassium phosphate]] KDP (KH<sub>2</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>), LiIO<sub>3</sub>, LiNbO<sub>3</sub>, and [[potassium titanyl phosphate]] KTP (KTiOPO<sub>4</sub>).

Perovskite materials have also recently emerged as promising second-harmonic-generation media, particularly in non-centrosymmetric hybrid and metal-free perovskites, where strong second-order optical nonlinearity and direct SHG have been reported in crystals, low-dimensional ferroelectric perovskites, and optical-fiber core geometries.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tsui |first1=Hei Chit Leo |last2=Sirbu |first2=Dumitru |last3=Alsaif |first3=Naseem |last4=Hill |first4=Nathan |last5=Tizzard |first5=Graham |last6=Docampo |first6=Pablo |last7=Healy |first7=Noel |title=Few-mode metal-free perovskite optical fiber with second-order optical nonlinearity |journal=APL Photonics |date=2024 |volume=9 |issue=3 |article-number=036106 |doi=10.1063/5.0186789 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ma |first1=Y. |last2=Wang |first2=J. |last3=Guo |first3=W. |last4=Han |first4=S. |last5=Xu |first5=J. |last6=Liu |first6=Y. |last7=Lu |first7=L. |last8=Xie |first8=Z. |last9=Luo |first9=J. |last10=Sun |first10=Z. |title=The First Improper Ferroelectric of 2D Multilayered Hybrid Perovskite Enabling Strong Tunable Polarization-Directed Second Harmonic Generation Effect |journal=Advanced Functional Materials |date=2021 |volume=31 |issue=37 |article-number=2103012 |doi=10.1002/adfm.202103012}}</ref>
